course.title: Maths Foundations
course.description: Rearrange an equation and know why each move is allowed. Read a straight line off a graph, and read a graph back into an equation.
course.audience: An adult returning to algebra who is comfortable with whole-number arithmetic.

paragraphs: Algebra is arithmetic with a gap left in it, in which a letter is written where an unknown number belongs and is reasoned about like any other number. People study it because one short line with a letter in it can describe every case of something at once, such as the fare for a taxi trip of any length or the amount left in a savings pot after any number of months, and because it is the shorthand of science and computing, so that little in either can be read far without it.

The course has six lessons in two parts. The first three, called Rearranging, show how to read a letter as a number not yet given, how to find that number by doing the same thing to both sides of an equation, and how to undo a calculation one step at a time. The last three, called Straight lines, place numbers on a grid and measure how steep a line is, and the final lesson links a line on the page to the equation that draws it.
Each lesson explains before it asks, so that a question appears only once the lesson has shown what the question needs.
outcomes: You'll be able to read an expression such as 3x − 4 as a calculation and work out its value for any number.
You'll be able to solve an equation such as 3x + 2 = 23 and say why each step keeps it true.
You'll be able to undo a calculation in the right order, including one with brackets.
You'll be able to find the gradient of a straight line from two points on it.
You'll be able to draw the line for y = mx + c and read its equation back off the line.
introduction.prerequisites: You should be comfortable with whole-number arithmetic, which is all the course assumes.

lessons.title: What a letter stands for

lead.text: Arithmetic often runs in a direction that hides the number being sought. A number has had something done to it, only the result is known, and the original has to be recovered by undoing what was done, which is possible because each operation has an opposite that restores the number it acted on.
If 8 has been added to a number and the result is 14, taking 8 away from 14 gives 6, and running the calculation forwards confirms it, since 6 plus 8 is 14.
In the same way, if a number has been doubled to give 18, halving 18 gives 9, because doubling 9 returns 18.

Each problem of this kind has a starting number that is not given, an operation applied to it, and a result that is, and the unknown is found by working from the result back through the operation. Algebra is a way of writing such problems down so that the writing holds whichever numbers are involved, and one more problem comes first, before any notation is introduced.

steps.headline: Giving the unknown number a name

lead.text: Writing out “the number” each time is clumsy, and arithmetic has long marked the gap with a box where the answer belongs. The problem just solved, written in that way, is:

The box stands for “some number”, and the equation asks which number fits. A box cannot be spoken aloud, however, and a problem with two gaps gives no way of telling them apart, so a letter takes its place:

The letter names the unknown number. It does not signify multiplication, and it need not be x, since any letter would serve equally well. Because the same letter can stand for a different number in a different problem, a letter used in this way is called a **variable**.

A line with an equals sign in the middle, like x + 5 = 12, is called an **equation**. The part before the sign is its left side and the part after it is its right side, and the equation claims that the two sides come to the same number. Read aloud as “some number, plus 5, makes 12”, it is the original problem again.
So far the letter has stood only for the answer, but it can also appear in a calculation whose result is not yet fixed, which is the subject of the next screen.

lead.text: Consider x + 5 on its own, with no equals sign and no result to find. It is a calculation with a gap in it: whatever number is put in for x, add 5. A calculation written with a letter in this way is called an **expression**.

An expression can be pictured as a machine, into which a number goes at one end and from which the result comes out at the other, after the machine has done what the expression says. The picture shows the machine for x + 5, and the slider chooses the number that goes in.

afterFigure.text: Putting in 3 gives 8, and putting in 10 gives 15. Replacing a letter with a number in this way is called **substituting**, and each substitution gives the value of the expression for that number.

The target beside the output is the 12 from the previous problem, so sliding the input until the machine reaches it finds the unknown number by trial, where before it was found by reasoning. Trial is slower, but it works for any expression, and later screens use it to test numbers.
A letter may also appear more than once in an expression, and the next screen shows what the machine does in that case.

lead.text: A letter that appears twice stands for the same number in both places, so the machine puts that number into every place the letter occurs. Substitute first, and then do the arithmetic.

workedSteps.text: Write 5 in place of each x.
Work out the sum.

lead.text: Until now a letter has appeared on its own or added to something, but one more convention turns up on almost every line of algebra and is worth learning early: a number written directly in front of a letter, with nothing between them, means multiplication. So 3x means 3 × x, three lots of x.

The × sign is left out because it is easily mistaken for the letter x, and the two are hard to tell apart in a line of working. The picture shows the machine for 3x, in which whatever goes in is multiplied by 3.

afterFigure.text: Putting in 4 gives 12, since 3 × 4 is 12, and not 34, which is what writing the 3 and the 4 side by side would suggest. Once a number replaces the letter, the multiplication sign has to be written back in.

Three lots of x is the same as x + x + x, which agrees with the previous screen: x is one number, and 3x is that number taken three times. Only multiplication is left out in this way, so the plus sign stays in 3 + x.
The next expression, 3x − 4, involves two steps, and so raises the question of which is done first.

lead.text: The expression 3x − 4 asks for two things to be done to x: it is multiplied by 3, and 4 is taken away. The order changes the result, as x = 5 shows. Multiplying by 3 first gives 15, and taking away 4 leaves 11, whereas taking away 4 first gives 1, and multiplying by 3 leaves 3.

So that every reader takes a line in the same way, mathematicians have agreed that multiplication is done before addition or subtraction unless brackets say otherwise. In 3x − 4 the multiplication therefore comes first, and by the same rule 2 + 3 × 4 equals 14, because the 3 × 4 is worked out before the 2 is added.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows both orders side by side. On the left, 5 goes into the multiply box and 15 comes out, after which 11 leaves the subtract box; on the right the boxes are swapped and the result is 3. The left-hand machine is the one the rule selects, and any expression can be run in the same way by listing its steps in the order the rule gives and writing down what leaves each box.
The next question supplies a machine and a number to run it with.

lead.text: Follow the two boxes in the order the rule gives.

reveal.text: The multiplication comes first, so 3 × 6 is 18, and subtracting 4 from that gives 14.

lead.text: Return to x + 5 = 12. Trying numbers in the machine showed that 7 fits, and fitting has a precise meaning: with 7 in place of x, the left side comes to 7 + 5, which is 12, and since the right side is already 12 the two sides agree.

A number that makes the two sides of an equation agree is called a **solution**, and finding it is called solving the equation. To test a suggested number, substitute it for the letter, work out the left side, and compare the result with the right side.

afterFigure.text: The picture is a balance, with the left side in one pan and the right side in the other. At x = 4 the left pan holds 9 and the right pan holds 12, so the balance tips and 4 is not a solution, and sliding x along shows that the balance levels at only one number.
A solution must make the two sides exactly equal, because close does not count, and the next screen carries out one test with some of the working supplied.

lead.text: The routine from the previous screen applies directly. The first line of working is supplied, and the next two are left for you to complete.

workedSteps.text: Replace x with 4.
Calculate the left side.
Compare with the right side, 9.

lead.text: The same routine applies to a new equation. The question asks first for the left side, and the comparison with the right side is left to you.

reveal.text: The routine is to substitute, work out the left side, and compare it with the right side. A solution must make the two sides exactly equal, and here the left side is 13, which is one more than 12.

lead.text: A taxi charges £3 to start and £2 for every mile, so for a trip of m miles the fare, in pounds, is 3 + 2m. Read the formula with the rule about order in mind.

lessons.orientation: Read a letter as a number not yet given, and test whether a number solves an equation by substituting it.
lessons.nextAction: Substitute a candidate, then compare both sides.

blocks.text: An equation such as x + 5 = 12 has a letter where a number should be, and it states something about that number: whatever it is, adding 5 to it gives 12. The number has not been given, but it is fixed all the same, and the letter is simply a way of referring to it before its value is known.

Most of algebra, from rearranging equations to drawing straight lines, depends on reading letters in this way, as a number with one definite value that is not yet known, and on being able to check whether a proposed value fits.

Once that reading is familiar, a line such as 3x − 4 stops looking like code and reads as a calculation waiting for a number, and testing a suggested value becomes a matter of substituting it and comparing the two sides.

intro.promise: By the end of the lesson you will read 3x − 4 as a calculation waiting for a number, and test whether a given number solves an equation.

recap.keyIdea: A letter stands for a number that has not been given, and a number solves an equation when substituting it for every copy of the letter makes the two sides come out equal.

blocks.text: Working back from 12 in x + 5 = 12 gave the unknown number 7. Machines for 3x − 4 and 3 + 2m were run by multiplying before adding or subtracting, and a suggested number was tested by working out the left side of the equation and comparing it with the right, which showed that 3 fails in 5x − 2 = 12 because its left side comes to 13.

recap.nextHook: Trying numbers finds a solution only if the right one happens to be tried, and no whole number satisfies 5x − 2 = 12, so the next lesson uses a balance to find the unknown number without guessing and shows why each step is allowed.

lessons.title: Keeping the balance

lead.text: Take scales that are level, with a bag of marbles and 6 loose marbles in the left pan and 10 marbles in the right, every marble weighing the same. Lifting the 6 loose marbles out of the left pan makes that pan rise and the scales tip, but taking 6 marbles out of the right pan as well brings them level again.
The left pan now holds only the bag and the right pan holds the 4 marbles left from the 10, so the bag must weigh the same as 4 marbles, and this has been found without opening it.

The reasoning rests on one rule: if two amounts are equal and the same amount is taken from each, what remains is still equal. Adding the same amount to each pan, or doubling or halving both, preserves the balance in the same way, whereas a change to one pan alone destroys it and makes any conclusion about the bag wrong.
The scales are a picture of something already familiar, since an equation is a pair of equal sides, and the next screen sets the scales and the equation side by side.

lead.text: Every marble weighs the same and the scales are level, so the number in the bag can be found by making the same change to both pans.

reveal.text: Taking the 3 spare marbles off both pans leaves the bag balanced against the remaining marbles, and the next screen writes that step down as an equation.

lead.text: To write the scales down, let x be the number of marbles in the bag. The left pan then holds x and 3 loose marbles and the right pan holds 11, so level scales give the equation:

The two pans are the two sides of the equation, and the equals sign says that they weigh the same. Taking 3 from both sides leaves x alone on the left and 11 − 3 on the right, which is the move made with the marbles, and it gives x = 8.

afterFigure.text: A move on one side only has a different effect. Taking 3 from the left side alone would give x = 11, but putting 11 into the original equation makes the left side 14 while the right side is still 11, so the balance is lost, because the move changed the problem.

The rule is therefore to do the same thing to both sides, and when this is done the new equation has exactly the same solution as the old one, so it can be used to simplify. The next question tests this.

lead.text: The balance shows 2x + 6 on the left and 18 on the right, and the aim is a simpler equation with exactly the same solution.

reveal.text: Whichever move was chosen, the test is whether it acted on both sides. Subtracting 6 from each side turns 2x + 6 = 18 into 2x = 12, which has the same solution in a simpler form.

lead.text: The scales show what may be done, but a plan is needed for getting x on its own, and the plan is to look at what has been done to x and undo it.

If 5 has been added to a number, taking 5 away restores the number, so adding and subtracting are opposites, and multiplying and dividing are opposites in the same way, since a number trebled and then divided by 3 returns to the number it began as.

An opposite move is called an **inverse operation**, and on the scales it can be pictured directly. If three identical bags balance 12 marbles, splitting each pan into three equal parts divides both sides by 3, and one bag then balances 4 marbles.

afterFigure.text: To get x alone, find what has been done to it and apply the inverse operation to both sides. One move is never allowed, which is dividing by 0, because every number multiplied by 0 gives 0, so nothing can undo the multiplication and recover the number that was started with.
The next question needs only one move.

lead.text: Four bags in one pan balance 20 marbles in the other, so the aim is to find the inverse operation that leaves x alone and to apply it to both sides.

reveal.text: The inverse of × 4 is ÷ 4, and applying it to both sides leaves x alone, so one move was enough.

lead.text: Most equations need more than one move. If four identical bags and 3 loose marbles sit in the left pan and 19 marbles in the right, the equation is:

The left pan cannot be split into four equal parts while loose marbles are mixed in with the bags, so the loose marbles must come off first, and the same number must come off the right pan. Subtracting 3 from both sides leaves four bags balancing 16 marbles:

afterFigure.text: Now the pan can be split, and dividing both sides by 4 leaves one bag balancing 4 marbles, so x = 4. The check is the one from the first lesson: with 4 in place of x the left side is 4 × 4 + 3 = 19, which matches the right side.
The next example writes the same two moves as equations, naming the move made at each line.

lead.text: Here the moves are written as equations, with each line naming a move and showing its result, and each move applied to both sides.

workedSteps.text: Subtract 2 from both sides. It undoes the + 2.
Now the × 3 has to go. Which move undoes it?
Divide both sides by 3.
Check in the original equation.

lead.text: The first line of working is supplied, and the last two lines are left for you to complete.

workedSteps.text: Subtract 8 from both sides.
Divide both sides by 2. Which x makes 2x = 12 true?
Check in the original equation.

steps.headline: When the numbers go below zero

lead.text: Every equation so far has contained only positive numbers, but equations can also contain minus signs and negative numbers, and the same two ideas apply. In 2x − 4 = −10, the 4 has been taken away from 2x, and the opposite of taking away is adding, so 4 is added to both sides.
The left side becomes 2x and the right side becomes −10 + 4. On a number line, starting at −10 and moving 4 steps to the right ends at −6, so −10 + 4 = −6 and the equation reads 2x = −6.

afterFigure.text: Dividing both sides by 2 finishes the job: −6 shared between two is −3, since a negative number divided by a positive number is negative, so x = −3. Putting −3 into the original equation confirms it, because 2 × (−3) is −6 and −6 − 4 is −10, which matches the right side.
A negative answer is allowed, since nothing in the method requires x to be positive, and the last question, which has a minus sign and a negative right side, is solved by the same moves.

lead.text: Here 9 is taken away from 3x and the right side is negative. Decide which move undoes the subtraction, and check the answer in the original equation.

lessons.orientation: Justify each step of a rearrangement by naming the operation applied to both sides.
lessons.nextAction: Unwind an expression by reversing the order its operations were applied in.

blocks.text: An equation says that its two sides are equal, and a pair of scales that sits exactly level says the same thing about the weights in its two pans, which makes the scales a useful way of seeing what can be done to an equation without changing its meaning.

In the last lesson an unknown number was found by trying values until one fitted, which is slow whenever the answer is not small. The scales suggest a method that needs no guessing, and it rests on a single question: what can be done to both pans while they stay level?
The answer, that the same change must be made to both sides, is the rule on which the solving of equations rests, and it is what allows an unknown number to be left alone on one side.

intro.promise: By the end of the lesson you will know why doing the same thing to both sides keeps an equation true, and will use that to solve for x.

recap.keyIdea: An equation stays true when the same thing is done to both sides, so the operations applied to x can be undone with their inverses until x stands alone.

blocks.text: The bag on the scales was found by taking the same number from both pans, and the same method with letters turned 3x + 2 = 23 into 3x = 21 and then x = 7. A minus sign made no difference to the method: in 3x − 9 = −15, adding 9 to both sides first led to x = −2.

recap.nextHook: In every example so far the order of the moves was given, so the next lesson explains why that order is the right one and how to choose it when x has more layers around it, including a part in brackets.

lessons.title: Undoing in the right order

lead.text: Take a number that has been trebled and then had 9 taken away, giving 21. The last job was taking away 9, so that comes off first, and 21 plus 9 is 30; the job before it was trebling, so that comes off next, and 30 divided by 3 is 10.

afterFigure.text: The picture runs the calculation forwards, trebling 10 to get 30 and then taking away 9 to get 21. The order of undoing matters, because undoing the jobs in the order they were done, dividing by 3 first and then adding 9, reaches 16, and trebling 16 and taking away 9 gives 39, which is not 21.

Whatever was done last has to be undone first, and each job is undone by its opposite, so reading a calculation from the result back to the start gives the number it began with. That is all that solving an equation with several moves comes to.

lead.text: This calculation has two jobs. Start from the result and take the jobs off, last job first.

reveal.text: The 4 was taken off first and the doubling was undone second. The next screen shows how to read the order of the jobs from an equation.

steps.headline: Reading the jobs from an equation

lead.text: An equation records its jobs in shorthand. In 2x + 5 = 11, the rule from the first lesson, that multiplication comes before addition, shows that the left side says to start with x, double it, and then add 5, and that the result of those jobs is 11.

afterFigure.text: Running this backwards from 11, the last job was adding 5, so 5 is taken away to give 6, and the job before it was doubling, so 6 is halved to give 3. The machine in the picture agrees, since putting in 3 gives 11.

On the scales these two backward steps are the two moves of the last lesson, subtracting 5 from both sides and then dividing both sides by 2, so the moves come in the reverse of the order of the jobs, and reading the left side shows where to begin. The next example writes the moves out as equations.

lead.text: Reading the jobs first, 5x − 3 means multiply by 5 and then take away 3, so the last job is taking away 3, and it comes off first.

workedSteps.text: The last job was − 3, so add 3 to both sides first.
Then undo the × 5: divide both sides by 5.
Check by running the machine forward.

lead.text: Read the jobs on x, take the last one off first, and then continue. The first line asks about the route, and the lines after it write the route out.

workedSteps.text: Read the jobs on x in 2x + 3, then choose the route that undoes them.
Subtract 3 from both sides. It undoes the last job.
Divide both sides by 2.
Check by running the machine forward.

lead.text: Name the last job first, undo it on both sides, and then undo the job before it.

reveal.text: The jobs were undone in the opposite order from the one in which the expression was built.

lead.text: In every equation so far the last job was easy to see, but brackets can hide it. Brackets are the curved marks around part of an expression, as in 3(x + 2), and they show that what is inside is worked out first and treated as a single package. A number written next to a bracket means multiplication, just as 3x does, so in 3(x + 2) the 2 is added to x first and the whole package is then multiplied by 3.

afterFigure.text: The jobs run in the order add 2, then multiply by 3, so multiplying by 3 is the last job and the first to be undone: dividing both sides by 3 opens the package, and the 2 is then taken away. In 3x + 2, by contrast, the 2 sits outside the multiplication and is added last, so brackets change which job comes last.
The same method works for any number of layers: list the jobs in the order that the expression builds them, starting inside the brackets, and take them off from the other end.

lead.text: Find the last job in 3(x + 2), take it off first, and then deal with what is inside the package.

reveal.text: The 3 multiplies the whole package, so it comes off first, and the + 2 comes off afterwards.

steps.headline: Answers that are not whole numbers

lead.text: In the first lesson, 3 was tested in 5x − 2 = 12 and the left side came to 13, which is one too many, and no whole number fits. The solution can be found now: the last job in 5x − 2 is taking away 2, so adding 2 to both sides gives 5x = 14, and both sides are then divided by 5.

afterFigure.text: Fourteen divided by 5 does not come out even, and is written as the fraction 14/5 or as the decimal 2.8. Running the machine forwards confirms it, since 5 × 2.8 is 14 and 14 − 2 is 12, and sliding the input in the picture to 2.8 meets the target.

Nothing in the method requires a whole-number answer. When the final division leaves a remainder, the answer is written as a fraction or a decimal, and a fraction such as 14/5 is exact, whereas a decimal is sometimes a rounded copy of it.

lead.text: Division is a job like any other: x ÷ 4 means x shared into four equal parts, and multiplying by 4 undoes it. As with every other job, each is undone by its opposite, last job first.

lessons.orientation: Unwind an expression by reversing the order its operations were applied in.
lessons.nextAction: Place a point from its coordinates and read coordinates back off a plotted point.

blocks.text: Every calculation is a sequence of jobs, each acting on the result of the one before, so reversing a calculation means reversing that sequence, with the last job undone first, because the effect of the first job is buried beneath the later ones.

An expression such as 2x + 3 is a short list of jobs done to a number, here doubling it and then adding 3, and to recover the number it started from the jobs are taken off in the opposite order, the addition first and the doubling second.

The equations of the last lesson named the first move, whereas this lesson gives the reason for it, so that the order can be worked out for any expression, including one such as 3(x + 2), where brackets make it less obvious.

intro.promise: By the end of the lesson you will undo a calculation one step at a time, last step first, to find the number that it started with.

recap.keyIdea: To find x, undo the operations applied to it in reverse order, last one first, doing the same to both sides at each step.

blocks.text: 5x − 3 = 12 was solved by adding 3 and then dividing by 5, and in 3(x + 2) = 21 the outside 3 was divided out before the 2 was taken off. The same method gave x = 2.8 for 5x − 2 = 12, a solution that trying whole numbers could never have reached.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson puts numbers on a grid, where a pair of them fixes a single point.

lessons.title: A point is a pair

lead.text: Lay a grid over the surface, with the lines one square apart and one crossing chosen as the starting point. That point is called the **origin**, and every set of directions begins from it. East is to the right and north is up, so a set of directions has two parts, first across and then up, and the number of squares in each part gives the two numbers.
The pair is written in brackets with a comma between, as in (3, 2), which reads as 3 across and 2 up. The origin itself is (0, 0), because no distance has been covered.

afterFigure.text: In the picture the point labelled A is at (3, 2), reached by counting three squares to the right of the origin and then two squares up. Every point on the grid has one pair and every pair names one point, so the pair works as an address.
One detail remains, which is what changes when the two numbers swap places.

lead.text: Directions of 4 squares across and 1 up, with the numbers swapped to give 1 across and 4 up, end at different points a long way from one another, so the pair has to be written in a fixed order that everyone shares, which is across first and then up.

The two numbers have names: the first is the **x-coordinate**, the number of squares across, and the second is the **y-coordinate**, the number of squares up, and together they are the **coordinates** of the point. In (4, 1) the x-coordinate is 4 and the y-coordinate is 1.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows (4, 1) and (1, 4), which use the same two numbers and land on different points. The order is easy to remember, because x comes before y in the alphabet, just as across comes before up.
That is enough to place a point from its pair, which is the next task.

lead.text: Start at the origin and take the across part of the pair first, then the up part.

reveal.text: The first number gave the move across and the second gave the move up, and swapping the numbers would have put B somewhere else.

lead.text: The two places in the question use the same two numbers in opposite orders, so compare them one number at a time.

reveal.text: The two places differ by one square across and one square up, so swapping the numbers moved the position to a different square.

lead.text: So far every move has gone to the right and up, but the grid does not stop at the origin, since there is ground to its left and below it. The number line supplies the way of describing it, because numbers below zero lie to the left of zero, and so a minus sign can mean the opposite direction.

A negative first number means a move to the left instead of the right, and a negative second number means a move down instead of up. The point (−5, 2) is 5 squares left of the origin and 2 up, while (3, −4) is 3 squares right and 4 down.

afterFigure.text: The sign belongs to its number and changes only the direction of that part of the move, while the size of the number still counts squares. A point with two minus signs, such as (−2, −3), lies to the left of the origin and below it, and it is still reached by a move across followed by a move up or down, with both parts going the other way.

lead.text: Here is a pair with a minus sign in it, placed one part at a time.

workedSteps.text: Start at the origin.
The x-coordinate is −4. Move 4 across, to the left.
The y-coordinate is 1. Move 1 up.
The x-coordinate is 4, so move 4 to the right.
Read the second number. What is the y-coordinate?
A y-coordinate of −2 means 2 squares down from there.

lead.text: The first number gives the position across, and its sign stays with it.

reveal.text: A minus sign on x means left of the origin, and it remains part of the coordinate.

lead.text: Two of the grid lines pass through the origin and matter more than the rest: the line that runs across is the **x-axis**, and the line that runs up and down is the **y-axis**. Each is a number line of its own, marked in squares from the origin.

A point on the x-axis has not moved up or down at all, so its y-coordinate is 0, as in (−4, 0). A point on the y-axis has not moved across, so its x-coordinate is 0, as in (0, 3), and the origin lies on both axes, which is why both of its numbers are 0.

afterFigure.text: With the axes named, any pair can be followed to its point and any point read back as a pair, and the final question tests both with a point on the far side of the origin.

lead.text: A point is marked at (−2, −3), measured from the origin at (0, 0), and movement is possible only along the grid lines, across first and then up or down.

lessons.orientation: Place a point from its coordinates and read coordinates back off a plotted point.
lessons.nextAction: Calculate a gradient from two points and say what its sign means.

blocks.text: A position on a flat surface can vary in two independent directions, so it takes two numbers to describe. Starting from an agreed point, the directions “3 squares east and then 2 squares north” identify exactly one spot, provided that both people begin from the same place and agree on which directions count.

One number fixes a position along a single line, but a surface has width as well as length, which is why map references, the squares of a chess board and the pixels of a screen are all named by pairs of numbers.
This lesson lays a grid over such a surface and places points from pairs of numbers, and it then extends the grid past its starting point, where numbers below zero are needed to say which way to go.

intro.promise: By the end of the lesson you will find any point on a grid from a pair of numbers, and write the pair for a point you can see.

recap.keyIdea: A point is a pair (x, y), with x across and y up, and a minus sign means left or down.

blocks.text: Directions of 3 across and 2 up place a point, and swapping the numbers sends it to a different square. The point (−4, 1) is placed by going 4 to the left and 1 up, the y-coordinate of (4, −2) is −2, and the point (−2, −3) is 5 squares from the origin along the grid lines.

recap.nextHook: Two of these points joined with a ruler give a line, and a line leans by some amount, so the next lesson puts a number on how steeply it leans.

lessons.title: How steep is it

lead.text: To compare the two paths, each climb is shared out evenly over its ground. On the steeper path, 30 metres of climb over 15 metres of ground gives 30 ÷ 15 = 2 metres of climb for each metre along, while on the gentler path the same 30 metres spread over 60 metres of ground gives 30 ÷ 60 = 0.5 metres for each metre along.

The comparison is now direct: 2 is four times as large as 0.5, so the first path is four times as steep. The number obtained by dividing the climb by the distance along the ground is called the **gradient**, and a gradient of 2 means that the path climbs 2 metres for every 1 metre covered.
Division is the whole method, and it applies to a hill, a ramp, a roof or a line on a grid, provided that the climb and the distance along can both be found.
Divide the climb by the distance along the ground, as was done for the two paths.

reveal.text: The climb divided by the distance along the ground is the gradient, and the next screen moves the same idea onto the grid.

steps.headline: Rise and run on the grid

lead.text: On a grid the two measurements need new names. Choosing two points on a line and moving from the first to the second, the change in y is called the **rise** and the change in x is called the **run**; these are the climb and the distance along in the language of the grid, so the gradient is the rise divided by the run.

In the picture the line goes from A = (1, 2) to B = (4, 5). Across the grid it moves from x = 1 to x = 4, so the run is 4 − 1 = 3, and up the grid it moves from y = 2 to y = 5, so the rise is 5 − 2 = 3.

afterFigure.text: Both are 3, so the gradient is 3 ÷ 3 = 1, which means that the line climbs one square for each square it moves across. The picture is not needed to obtain these numbers, because subtracting the coordinates of the two points gives the rise and the run, and the picture only shows what the subtraction means.

lead.text: The rise is how far up the line goes from A to B, so compare the heights of the two points.

reveal.text: That vertical change is the rise, and dividing it by the run gives the gradient.

lead.text: The picture helps when the points are close together, but the subtraction works anywhere. The rise is the second point's y-coordinate minus the first point's, and the run is found in the same way from the x-coordinates, so from (2, 3) to (5, 9) the rise is 9 − 3 = 6, the run is 5 − 2 = 3, and the gradient is 6 ÷ 3 = 2.

The two subtractions must be taken in the same order, because reversing only one of them gives the wrong sign: a rise of 6 over a run of −3 would give −2, although the line really climbs. Each subtraction goes from the first point to the second, so that both describe the same movement.
The next example takes a pair of points through the whole calculation, one line at a time.

workedSteps.text: Rise: subtract the y-coordinates, second minus first.
Run: subtract the x-coordinates in the same order.
Divide the rise by the run.
Rise: second y minus first y.
Run: second x minus first x.
Divide the rise by the run.

lead.text: So far every line has climbed as it moved to the right, but a line can also fall. For the points (0, 6) and (3, 0), y drops from 6 to 0 in going from the first point to the second, so the rise is 0 − 6 = −6, the run is 3 − 0 = 3, and the gradient is −6 ÷ 3 = −2.

A negative rise means that the line goes down, so the sign of the gradient shows which way the line leans: a line that climbs as it moves right has a positive gradient, and a line that falls has a negative one. A flat line has a rise of 0, and 0 divided by any run is 0, so its gradient is 0.

afterFigure.text: The size of the gradient, ignoring its sign, shows how steep the line is, so a gradient of 3 climbs faster than a gradient of 1/2, as the steeper path climbed faster than the gentler one, and a gradient of −3 falls as quickly as 3 climbs.

lead.text: This line falls as it moves right, so take both subtractions in the same order and keep track of the signs.

reveal.text: The rise is negative and the run is positive, so the gradient is negative, as the falling line showed.

lead.text: Not every line is steep, and the rise and the run should be kept separate until the final division.

lessons.orientation: Calculate a gradient from two points and say what its sign means.
lessons.nextAction: Draw the line of y = mx + c from its two numbers, and recover them from a drawn line.

blocks.text: Any two points on a grid have a straight line between them, and that line leans by some amount. The lean is easiest to understand on a slope, where a path that climbs 30 metres while covering 15 metres of ground is far steeper than one that climbs the same 30 metres while covering 60 metres.
Neither the climb nor the ground covered says how steep a path is on its own, because steepness depends on the two together.
This lesson turns that dependence into a single number, first for the paths and then for lines on the grid of the last lesson, including lines that fall and lines that stay level.

intro.promise: By the end of the lesson you will find a line's gradient from two points, and say what its sign tells you.

recap.keyIdea: The gradient is the rise divided by the run, with both taken in the same direction, so a rising line has a positive gradient, a falling line a negative one, and a flat line a gradient of 0.

blocks.text: Two paths were compared by sharing the climb over the ground, and the line through (1, 2) and (3, 12) has gradient 10 ÷ 2 = 5. The line through (−2, 3) and (2, −1) falls, and its gradient is −1.

recap.nextHook: A gradient says how steeply a line leans, but two lines with the same gradient can lie side by side at different heights, so the next lesson shows what fixes where a line sits and how both numbers go into one equation.

lessons.title: From equation to line

lead.text: The candle's height can be written down each hour. At the start it is 12 centimetres, after 1 hour it has lost 2, which leaves 10, and after 2 hours it has lost 4 and stands at 8.

The pattern is a loss of 2 centimetres for every hour that passes, so after any number of hours the loss is 2 times that number, and the height left is the starting 12 minus the loss. After 5 hours the loss is 2 × 5 = 10, which leaves 12 − 10 = 2 centimetres.

Calling the number of hours x and the height y, as on the grid of the last two lessons, gives the rule y = 12 − 2x, which contains two numbers: the 12 where the candle starts and the 2 that says how fast it burns.
The rule from the previous screen takes the amount burned away from the starting height.

reveal.text: The candle loses 3 × 2 = 6 centimetres, which comes off the 12, and the next screen puts these heights on a graph.

lead.text: Plotting the heights with the hours across and the height up gives one point for each hour. After 1 hour the candle is at (1, 10), after 2 hours at (2, 8), and so on down to (5, 2). The grid in the picture is only 10 squares high, so the points start at the first hour, but the pattern carries on past the edge.

afterFigure.text: The points lie on a straight line. Each hour across lowers the height by 2, so the gradient of the line is −2, which is the burning rate with a minus sign because the height falls, and following the line back to the y-axis shows that it crosses at 12, the height at the moment the candle is lit.
The height at which a line crosses the y-axis is called its **intercept**, and two numbers fix the candle's line: the gradient says how steeply it leans and the intercept says where it starts.

steps.headline: Writing the line as an equation

lead.text: Putting the two numbers into the rule gives the candle's line as y = −2x + 12, in which −2 is the gradient and 12 is the intercept. Other lines follow the same pattern with different numbers, so the pattern is written with letters as y = mx + c, where m stands for the gradient and c for the intercept, and each line has its own pair of values.

To see why c is the intercept, put x = 0 into the equation: the mx term becomes m × 0, which is 0, so y is just c, and the point (0, c) lies on the line exactly where it crosses the y-axis. For y = 3x + 4 the line crosses at height 4 and climbs 3 for every step across.
The line meets the y-axis where x is 0, so put x = 0 into the equation.

reveal.text: With x = 0 the x term vanishes, so y is just c, which is the intercept.

steps.headline: Drawing a line from its equation

lead.text: An equation also shows how to draw its line. A value is chosen for x and substituted into the equation, and y is worked out with the multiplication done before the addition, so that the resulting pair is a point on the line. For y = 2x − 3, x = 0 gives y = 2 × 0 − 3 = −3, so (0, −3) is a point, and x = 3 gives y = 2 × 3 − 3 = 3, so (3, 3) is another.

afterFigure.text: Two points are enough, because only one straight line passes through both, so they can be joined with a ruler and the line extended either way. The gradient from the two points checks the result, since (3 − (−3)) ÷ 3 = 2, which is the 2 in the equation.
Substitution also works the other way: when y = 2x and y is 14, the equation is 2x = 14, and dividing both sides by 2 gives x = 7.

steps.headline: Find two points on y = 3x − 1, then draw the line.

workedSteps.text: Choose x = 0. This gives the intercept.
Choose x = 2.
Check the gradient from the two points.

steps.headline: Find the point on y = −x + 3 where x = 2.

workedSteps.text: Replace x with 2. The minus sign stays in front.
Work it out. What is y?

steps.headline: Reading the equation off a line

lead.text: The reverse direction runs from a line to its equation. For a line through (0, 5) and (2, 1), the point on the y-axis, (0, 5), gives the intercept at once, so c = 5, and the gradient comes from the rise and the run: from (0, 5) to (2, 1) the rise is 1 − 5 = −4 and the run is 2 − 0 = 2, so m = −4 ÷ 2 = −2.

afterFigure.text: The line is therefore y = −2x + 5, and putting the other point back in checks it, since x = 2 gives y = −2 × 2 + 5 = 1, which matches (2, 1). A line that falls always has a negative m, as the candle's line did.

lead.text: Read c from the point where x is 0, and then use both points to find the gradient.

reveal.text: The point on the y-axis gave c and the two points gave m, and these two numbers are the whole equation.

lead.text: A container holds 2 litres and gains 0.5 litres every minute, so after x minutes its volume in litres is y = 0.5x + 2, in which the intercept is the starting amount and the gradient is the rate.

lessons.orientation: Draw the line of y = mx + c from its two numbers, and recover them from a drawn line.

blocks.text: A candle that stands 12 centimetres tall and burns down by 2 centimetres every hour has heights of 12, 10, 8, 6 and so on at successive hours, and the whole list is described by one short rule.

The last lesson left a loose end: a gradient says how steeply a line leans, but two lines with the same gradient can lie side by side at different heights. The candle shows both halves of a line, since it starts at some height and falls at some rate, and those two numbers are all that is needed to describe it.

The candle's heights lie on a straight line, and the equation of that line has the same form as the equation of every other line, which makes it possible both to draw a line from its equation and to read the equation back from a line.

intro.promise: By the end of the lesson you will draw the line of y = mx + c from its two numbers, and read both numbers back off a line.

recap.keyIdea: A line y = mx + c is fixed by two numbers, c where it crosses the y-axis and m its gradient.

blocks.text: The candle that started at 12 centimetres and burned 2 an hour has the line y = −2x + 12. The line y = 3x − 1 was drawn through (0, −1) and (2, 5), and y = 2x − 2 was read off the line through (0, −2) and (2, 2).
